title: How do I add static pages to WordPress?

content:
# Static HTML in WordPress: Architecture, Routing, and SEO Implications Integrating standalone static files like `products.html` into a dynamic WordPress environment requires bypassing the default theme loading mechanism. By default, WordPress expects all front-end content to be rendered via PHP templates located in your active theme directory. If you simply upload an HTML file to your web server's root folder alongside your theme, WordPress will likely ignore it unless explicitly told otherwise. To make `products.html` accessible and editable within the CMS structure, you must configure a custom route or modify the template hierarchy. ## The Custom Template Approach The most robust method for adding a static page without breaking your existing theme architecture is to create a custom PHP template file. This approach allows WordPress to render the HTML while maintaining access to standard functions like `wp_head()`, `get_the_title()`, and navigation menus. To implement this, place an HTML file named `products.html` in your theme's root folder (e.g., `wp-content/themes/your-theme`). Then, create a corresponding PHP file named `product.php` in the same directory. WordPress follows a strict template hierarchy; when it detects a request for a page slug like "products", it will check for `product.php` before falling back to `page.php` or `index.php`. In `product.php`, you can embed your static HTML directly, but you must wrap the content appropriately: ```php

Our Products

Static content description...

``` This structure ensures that your custom styles and layout are preserved while allowing WordPress to handle the header, footer, and dynamic menu items. You can then assign this template to a specific page in the WordPress admin by editing the "Page Attributes" section under the Template dropdown. ## Configuring Permalinks and URLs A common pitfall when introducing static files is URL consistency. If you attempt to serve `products.html` directly via a browser without WordPress intervention, you risk creating duplicate content issues or conflicting routing rules. To integrate it seamlessly, you should map the HTML file to a standard WordPress page slug. In your WordPress dashboard, create a new Page titled "Products" and set its permalink structure to `/products/`. Ensure that your `.htaccess` file (for Apache) or `web.config` (for IIS) is configured correctly to handle static files if you intend to serve them directly without the PHP wrapper. However, for full integration with menus and dynamic content, keeping the PHP wrapper is preferred. If you choose to serve the raw HTML file directly, you must ensure that WordPress does not try to rewrite the URL to a PHP script first. This often involves adding specific rules to your `.htaccess` file to exclude certain paths from rewriting: ```apache RewriteRule ^products\.html$ - [L] ``` This rule tells the server to stop processing and serve `products.html` directly if requested. However, this creates a disconnect; your WordPress menu pointing to `/products/` will likely redirect to `/products.html`, which can confuse search engines. The PHP template method avoids this by keeping the URL structure clean (`/products/`) while utilizing the static file's content. ## Trade-offs and Best Practices The decision to use a custom template versus serving raw HTML depends on your maintenance strategy. Using a custom PHP template allows you to edit the page content directly within the WordPress admin panel, enabling version control via plugins like Jetpack or simple text editors. This is highly recommended for collaborative environments. Conversely, if `products.html` contains complex JavaScript that needs to load before any WordPress headers are processed, serving it as a raw static file might be necessary. In such cases, you must manually manage the URL mapping and ensure no canonical tags conflict between your static page and the dynamic WordPress site map. For developers looking to streamline their workflow or need advanced routing capabilities beyond standard WordPress themes, exploring frameworks like Laravel can offer more granular control over static asset management and routing logic. This is particularly useful if you are building a larger application where strict separation of concerns is required.
